AlternateTargets: to cling to grass and attach to trees
Senses.Explanation: Literally, to cling to grass and attach to trees. The phrase occurs 128 times in 71 allowlisted texts. Chan masters repeatedly apply the plant-clinging image as a rebuke. Ying'an Tanhua lists striking the bench, raising the whisk, blinking, raising the eyebrows, pointing east and west, and moving the lips and tongue, then says that these still do not escape clinging to grass and attaching to trees. Chijue Daochong applies it to making a livelihood on circumstances and objects and seeking clever explanations in principle and nature. Yuanwu Keqin calls people who talk of gain and loss ‘spirits clinging to grass and attaching to trees’ (說得說失得麼。若有恁麼。盡是依草附木精靈). In his case commentary, Yuanwu sets the phrase alongside feeling along a fence and wall, while Gulin Qingmao calls an interlocutor's raised fist precisely such clinging. The bearer can be called a spirit or a person, and the criticized support changes with the passage; the headword still names the same act of dependence.
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense. No plain botanical deployment appeared in the surveyed defining contexts. Different bearers and different grammatical surroundings do not create another referent. The Zen-specific bend is the regular use of the plant-clinging image as a teaching-seat rebuke for dependence on words, gestures, objects, or circumstances.
